s: Apex Insights: Every facility’s numbers, and a nudge when one slips
A group of nursing homes kept its numbers in Power BI, Microsoft’s reporting tool.
Apex Insights puts every report behind one front door, and warns the right leader when a facility’s number slips.
My role Lead UI/UX Designer
Client A skilled nursing group
Platforms Desktop web and Power BI
Scope Information architecture, portal screens, the report layout system, and client wireframe reviews
Deliverables 131 portal screens and 8 Power BI report layouts

I worked with the client’s BI team and two developers, and reported to their operations director.
The hardest part came before I drew a single screen: working out what the client actually needed.
Here’s how the work was split.

s: The reports existed.
Getting to the right one at the right moment didn’t.
The group already had Power BI reports for census (how many beds are filled), staffing, payroll and revenue.
The data wasn’t missing.
The problem was finding the right report in time, and noticing a slipping number before it turned into a cost.
Who
Executives, facility administrators and directors of nursing across a group of skilled nursing facilities.
What went wrong
Census, staffing, payroll and revenue lived in separate Power BI reports.
To find a number, you had to know which report it was in.
Why it mattered
Staffing below target means overtime, agency cost, or a short shift.
A number noticed three days late means three days of that cost.
The UX challenge
Give every report one front door, and bring problems to people before they go looking.
Step 1 A number is needed
Today’s staffing at one facility, before the morning meeting.
What it took Asked for by a leader
Step 2 Find the report
Know which Power BI report holds it, then open it.
What it took Which report has hours per patient day (HPPD)?
Each report laid out its own way
Step 3 · where it slowed Filter and export
Set the facility and the date, then export it to send on.
What it took Filters set again in every report A file emailed to whoever asked
Step 4 · where it stopped Nobody is told
When a number crosses a line, nobody hears about it until someone looks.
What it took No threshold, so no alert The next look could be next week
A staffing number that drifted on Monday could go unnoticed until someone happened to look again.
This is pieced together from the brief and the client’s answers in the first review, since how people found reports before the portal wasn’t documented.
The brief listed features, but not what they were for
The brief named features like Alerts and File storage, but never said what job they did.
Before laying out the portal, I wanted to know what each one was for.
So I ran wireframe reviews with the client’s leadership and their BI team, and went through every Power BI report page myself.
Who I worked with, and how
Client leadership
Which numbers they check each morning
The client’s BI team
Data models and report logic
Engineering
Build, sign-on and embedding
Wireframe reviews
Two rounds, March 26 and 29
Report audit
Every Power BI page, census to finance
Not available
Usability sessions, analytics, user interviews
What the first wireframes left open
The March 26 wireframes gave every feature in the brief a place.
Writing my questions right on those frames showed which features didn’t have a job yet.
The red outlines mark what each question was about.
What kind of content comes under it?” Alerts was a menu item with nothing defined inside it.
2 “What is file storage?” It sat under Subscriptions and sounded like a folder nobody needs.
3 “Will the dashboard tab have only one interactive dashboard?” One shared view for an executive and a director of nursing.
4 Tiles counted reports, not facilities “12 dashboards, 8 reports” says where to look, not how a facility is doing.
Two more questions were on the report wireframes: why two sets of action buttons, and whether a dashboard widget needs every action.
Both led to Decision 1.

Each answer changed what got built.
Evidence Insight Design decision

Decision 1

March 26 home

Decision 2

Questions on the frames
Leaders don’t go looking for problems.
The numbers have to come to them.
Schedules for the routine, thresholds for the exceptions.
Decision 3
Different people built the report pages, each with its own header and filters.
Power BI report pages
Learning one report should mean you can read the rest.
One layout for every Power BI report.
Decision 4
One home for every number, and alerts for the exceptions
By the end of the reviews, two needs were clear.
Every report had to be easy to reach and read.
And leaders shouldn’t have to go looking for problems.
That gave me one principle, and it shaped the four decisions below.
The principle
Give every number one home, and send the exceptions to the people who own them.
The routine the design supports
An alert arrives
It names the facility, the number and the line it crossed
Open the report
Last refresh, tabs and filters sit where they sit in every report
Drill into HPPD
By shift and position, with a way back
Share it on
A subscription from the same menu, delivered to file storage
One place for every action
In my first wireframes, each report carried the portal’s buttons and Power BI’s own controls.
Clone and Rename showed up twice, as different buttons in different places.
I asked the client why, right on the frame, and pushed for one place for every action.
The BI team wanted to keep Power BI’s own controls, since leaders already knew them.
We met in the middle: Power BI’s icons stayed for pin and full screen.

In the final screens, every report has the same corner: pin and full screen as icons, and everything else in one menu, including export, print, subscribe, subscriptions for others, favorite, refresh, and, for people with permission, edit and delete.
Options
Keep both sets of actions · rebuild every action in the portal · one corner with Power BI’s actions inside it
Decision
Pin and full screen as icons, everything else in one menu, the same on every report.
Trade-off
Some Power BI options stay hidden from everyday users.
Result
Approved by the client.
Not tested with users.
Round 1 · Two sets
Portal Favorite Clone Rename Subscribe
Power BI Export Clone Rename Print
When the same action lives in two places, people have to learn two behaviors, and nobody knows which one is the “real” one.
Final · One corner
Every report Pin Full screen ⋮ Menu
One corner, the same on every report.
Widgets on a dashboard open their report; they don’t carry their own actions.
Simplified from the Round 1 wireframes.
Clone and rename are the documented duplicates.
The two actions people use while reading stay visible as icons.
Export and print, for the person who still has to send a file.
For yourself, or create a subscription for your team.
Edit and delete sit at the bottom, apart from everything else.
Let the reports have the width
My first home screen was a dense grid with a fixed sidebar.
But Power BI tables need width, and that sidebar took 224px of it on every screen.
In the March 29 round, I tried wider tiles with the sidebar as an overlay.
The final home keeps that idea: an icon rail that expands only when you need it.
Options
Keep the fixed sidebar · move navigation to a top bar · a rail that collapses to icons
Decision
A collapsed icon rail and wider tiles, so Power BI tables get the width.
Trade-off
Navigation is one move away, not always in view.
Result
Approved by the client.
Not tested with users.
March 26 · Round 1
A fixed sidebar with labels, and tiles that show dashboard and report counts.
March 29 · Round 2
Wider tiles, and the sidebar shrinks to icons.
The report list also lost its last and next run columns.
Final · Chosen theme
A collapsed icon rail, color-coded module tiles, and Add Report for admins.
Bring the numbers to people
My “What is alerts?” question had a simple answer in the end: leaders don’t want to open a portal just to check whether something’s wrong.
So the portal goes to them.
Subscriptions send a report on a schedule and can be paused.
File storage keeps every run with its status.
Alerts go out when a facility crosses a line.
The routine goes on a schedule.
Only the exceptions interrupt anyone.
Options
Email every report on a schedule · alert on every change · schedules for the routine, thresholds for exceptions
Decision
Subscriptions for the routine, and three alert levels tied to a line per facility.
Trade-off
Someone at the client has to own each threshold, or alerts become noise.
Result
Approved by the client.
Same-day action on alerts isn’t measured yet.
Source Data refresh
Census, staffing and payroll refresh overnight
The routine Subscription
A report on a schedule, to one person or a team
Lands in File storage
Every run: in queue, in progress, completed or error
The exception Threshold
Set per facility, like an HPPD target
Becomes Alert
Informational, warning or critical
Reaches The right leader
Same day, in the portal and by email
All, informational, warning and critical, each with a count.
“Facility E staffing: nursing HPPD is 3.64, below the 3.80 target for the third day in a row.” Nobody has to open a report to know what happened.
Red for critical and amber for warning, next to an icon and words, so color isn’t the only cue.
Mark all as read, or one at a time from the menu.
Facility names and thresholds are sample data in the screens, not the client’s real targets.
Subscriptions: last and next run, Paused when switched off.
File storage: every run with its status, and an error that says why.
One layout for every Power BI report
Different people had built the Power BI reports, each with their own header and filters.
I designed one layout for all of them, so once you’ve learned one report, you can read the rest.
Same header, same filters, same chips, and drill-throughs (clicking a number to see its detail) that always have a way back.
Options
Each builder lays out their own · one fixed template · one shared frame with free content
Decision
One shared frame: refresh, tabs, filter chips, headline numbers and expandable rows, always in the same places.
Trade-off
Report builders give up some freedom.
Result
When the data was last updated, at the top of every report.
Dashboard or reports, then the pages of this report.
Applied filters stay visible and clear in one click.
The few numbers that matter, before any table.
Each facility opens to its detail in place.
Drill-through, with a way back
Staffing breaks HPPD down by shift and position, the way a director of nursing thinks about a shift.
The header stays the same, and Back returns to the summary with the filters kept.
What was checked, and what still needs testing
We didn’t run usability testing on this project, and I never met facility staff directly; everything came through leadership and the BI team.
That’s the first gap I’d close.
Here’s what was checked instead, what’s still wrong, and how I’d test the rest.
Design Finding Design response Result
Approved screens
A copy check after sign-off found placeholder text and typos.
Each one listed so it can be fixed before the build.
Fix not confirmed

What shipped, and how I’d know it worked
The portal was built and handed over to the client’s team, who were rolling it out to facilities when my part ended.
There’s no usage data yet.
So I keep three things apart: what was delivered, what the client approved, and what I expect to happen but can’t show yet.
Status Target Outcome
Approved Portal screens
131 final portal screens, approved by the client.
Approved Power BI report layouts
8 layouts on one shared frame, with shared components for the portal and reports.
Not measured Fewer report requests, and exceptions seen the same day
Expected, but there’s no usage data yet to show it.
What I would measure next
Alerts acted on the same day The number I’d hold it to: time from a critical alert to read and flagged.
Time to find a report From search or home to the report opening.
Alerts read vs ignored Per level, to see whether thresholds are tuned or turning into noise.
Report runs that fail Error vs completed runs in file storage.
Three things I took away from this project
The most useful thing I did on this project wasn’t a screen.
It was asking questions early.
These are the habits I’ve kept.
Lesson Then, on this project Now
Alerts and file storage were just names in a brief until I asked what they were for.
My first review is always questions, written next to the screens they’re about.
Lorem ipsum and typos like “Exceutive” and “Unable to Complie” reached approved screens.
I run a copy check before anything goes for sign-off.
The screens were approved with no way to see whether they worked.
The number to track is agreed in the same meeting as sign-off.
A future direction: one sign-in for both portals
The client also runs a second portal for day-to-day management.
The next design joins the two behind one sign-in, so a leader can go from a number to an action without logging in twice.
The weekly staffing module, with drill-throughs for HPPD, overtime, agency and spend, is already designed in the same layout.

s: A ten-year-old portal, used at very different speeds
Customers and partners use the licence portal to activate keys, assign product packs and keep track of their licences.
It’s a ten-year-old Java application with fewer than 30 pages.
It works, but little of it is documented, and it doesn’t work on a tablet.
An earlier attempt to replace it had failed, so IGEL froze it and split the rebuild into two phases.
Phase 1 was a new front end, with no change to the business logic underneath.
Customers
Open it about once a year, to renew.
Many never become fluent, and some are covering for a colleague.
Partners and MSPs
Use it many times a day.
Reporting means an Excel export, which IGEL’s CIO called “very cumbersome”.
IGEL’s own team
Power users who can change any licence for any customer, and need a record of who changed what.
The UX challenge
Make it clear for the once-a-year customer, without slowing down the partner who lives in it.
A renewal, before the redesign
Step 1 A renewal is due
An email says a subscription is about to expire.
Joachim last logged in months ago.
What it took Remember the portal exists Find the login
Step 2 Find the right company
Switching company in the old portal means a right-click menu, which few people expect on a website.
What it took Find the company Check the Global Account ID
Step 3 · where it slowed Read the packs
Packs show as codes like EMP, TER and WE, with statuses such as BOOKED and BOOKED_ILP.
What it took Decode the abbreviations Guess what each status means
Step 4 · where it stopped Act on it
Every row has the same small arrow.
Nothing says which pack needs renewing first.
What it took No clear next step Risk of a duplicate licence
A once-a-year admin could finish a renewal still unsure whether they’d done it right.
Pieced together from the old portal, IGEL’s personas and its support team’s feedback.
The right-click menu comes from IGEL’s CIO, who walked us through the portal on our call.
I started from IGEL’s own research
IGEL’s UX lead had already run workshops, written two personas, mapped five use cases and audited the portal in 23 pages.
He was open that none of it had been tested with users; it came from internal sources.
Two more inputs filled the gaps: a page-by-page list of fixes from IGEL’s support team, and the CIO’s answers on our call.

The two people IGEL designed for
Maria
Fills in for two weeks
An IT admin who has never used IGEL products.
She’s covering while Joachim is on leave, doesn’t know where to find anything, and isn’t even aware she needs to do more than press “remove device”.
“I just need something that shows me what to do, step by step, so I don’t miss anything while I’m filling in.”
Joachim
Rarely uses the portal
An IGEL admin who opens the portal so rarely he never becomes fluent in it.
He licenses devices, swaps damaged hardware and runs renewals, and has to avoid creating duplicate licences.
“I need a system that tells me exactly what to do next, alerts me when something needs my attention, and helps me avoid mistakes, because I don’t use this every day.”

What changed my thinking
The draft was cleaner.
It wasn’t smarter.
IGEL’s 2.0 draft applied the audit well: a neutral palette, the company in the header, a table for licences.
But it still showed you numbers and left you to work out what they meant.
The CIO asked for something “more intelligent” than endless lists.
That became the brief I gave myself.
Keep IGEL’s audit, and add the next step
The seven audit moves were right, and Phase 1 couldn’t touch the business logic anyway.
So I kept every move and every feature.
What I added was a layer on top: a portal that notices what needs doing and says so, in words a once-a-year admin understands.
The principle
Design for how often people actually use it.

s: I led four designers, and started with what they’d all share
Four designers were about to work on six services at the same time.
My job was to keep them all following the same rules.
So before anyone started a service, I designed the parts they’d all share.
Every week I ran a review where we checked new screens against those rules.

s: Patients picked a doctor and a time, and only then found out they couldn’t book
A lot of patients book with insurance.
But the app only checked the hospital’s rules after they’d already chosen a doctor and a time.
Some of those checks were dead ends, and the only way forward was a phone call.
Who
Patients booking for themselves or family, many paying with insurance.
What went wrong
Rules about the policy, Emirates ID, profile and referrals only showed up after a time was picked.
The price only showed up after booking.
Why it mattered
Many blocked bookings ended in “Please contact our call center.” Unverified policies risked rejected claims.
The UX challenge
Show the hospital’s rules while the patient can still change their mind.
Step 1 Find a doctor
Specialty, language, the next free slot.
Checked here Nothing checked yet
Step 2 Pick a time
The slot is held for 10 minutes while the patient pays.
Checked here Nothing checked yet
Step 3 · where it stopped Checkout
Patient, payment method, then Book.
Checked here New policy still being verified Emirates ID has expired Profile blocked or under review Specialty needs a GP visit first
Step 4 After booking
Booked, but the price isn’t known yet.
Checked here Fee created only after the insurer replies
Nothing was checked while the patient was still choosing.
By the time a rule showed up, the doctor and time were already set, and some rules left only one option: call.
Each screen worked.
The order didn’t.
I had no usability sessions or analytics to work from.
So I started with what I could check: every approved screen, and the people who owned the rules.
That’s when it clicked.
The rules were split across three teams, and nobody could see the whole booking.
Who I worked with, and how
Teleconsult team
GP hours, and which specialties need a GP first
Insurance team
Policy rules, and when a new policy is verified
Registration team
When a profile goes into review or gets blocked
Scope discussions
With all three teams
State audit
Every approved state, screen by screen
Not available
Usability sessions, analytics, call-center logs
So the insights below come from the audit and those conversations, not from watching patients.
What patients actually saw
I went through the approved screens as a patient would.
The red outline marks the message each one shows.
Policy still pending
Doctor and time already set, then a note to switch to Self Pay.
Emirates ID expired
A banner on the booking screen asks for an ID update before a video consult.
Profile blocked
Shown on the doctor page once a time is picked, pointing to the call center.
GP referral needed
An insurance pop-up says the visit needs a referral letter from a GP.

approved states ended in some version of “Please contact our call center.” These include a blocked profile, a profile under review, a technical failure, and a GP visit that could only be booked by phone.

Audit of approved states
Patients committed before the app knew whether they could book.
Check each rule at the point where it can still change the choice.
Decision 1
Many states ended in “Please contact our call center.”
Same audit
The app treated problems patients could fix the same as ones only staff could fix.
Route each blocker by who can fix it.
Decision 2
The hospital system creates the fee only after the insurer replies.
Constraint from the scope discussions
The price can’t be a condition for booking.
It has to show up as a status.
Show Under Process, then send the fee as a notification.
Decision 4
Six services needed the same identity, insurance and checkout.
Project scope
If each flow designed its own rules, they’d drift apart.
Design checkout once, and let each service add to it.
Decision 3
Check things while the patient can still choose
The audit made one thing clear.
No single screen was broken.
The problem was when each rule showed up.
So I started every decision with one question: what’s the earliest point this check can still change what the patient picks?
The principle
Check each rule at the first moment it can still change the patient’s choice.
What booking looks like now
Find a doctor
Age, gender and GP-first rules filter the list
Pick a time
The slot is held for 10 minutes while the patient pays
Check out

After booking
The fee arrives as a notification, with one tap to pay
Four insurance states, each with a next step
An insurer can take hours to verify a new policy, and Aster can’t speed that up.
The insurance team’s first instinct was to block every pending policy.
I walked them through what that means for a patient booking a video call in the next hour, and proposed drawing the line by time until the visit instead.
They set it at four hours, based on how long verification usually takes.
Options
Block every pending policy · let every pending policy through · draw the line by time until the visit
Decision
More than four hours away, book now and the fee follows.
Closer than that, switch to Self Pay.
Trade-off
One more rule patients have to understand.
Result
Shipped.
Pending bookings that end in a rejected claim aren’t measured yet.
Patient picks a time and pays with insurance

Nothing to fix.

Pending · more than 4 hours away Book now, the fee follows

The note explains, and the copay reads Under Process.
The insurer replies before the visit and the fee arrives as a notification.
Decision 4 shows what happens next.
Pending · within 4 hours Steered to Self Pay
The insurer may not reply in time.
The policy shows Pending, a note says to tap Self Pay, and Book waits until they do.
Tap Self Pay and keep the slot, or go back and choose a time more than four hours away.
Not covered Self Pay, with the reason
The default policy doesn’t cover this consult.
A note says so, and Book waits until Self Pay is picked.
Tap Self Pay, or tap Change to use another linked policy.
These are the four insurance states from the approved file.
Every one ends with something the patient can do.
Sending each problem to whoever can fix it
An expired ID, a blocked profile and a server failure all ended the booking the same way.
But they’re very different problems.
One generic error would send a patient to the phone over an ID they could update in a minute.
Options
One error, one phone number · a retry or appeal on every blocker · route by who can fix it
Decision
If the patient can fix it, give them a button.
If only staff can, name the call center.
If the app failed, offer a call.
Trade-off
Three patterns instead of one, so more states to design and QA.
Result
Shipped.
Call-center contacts per booking aren’t measured yet.

Update Now sits in the banner.
After the update, the patient comes back to the same booking.
Only a person can fix it Blocked profile

No button.
A blocked profile needs someone with hospital records, so the screen names the call center instead.

No retry button that fails the same way twice.
One checkout for every service
Consults came first, and five more services were right behind.
Each needed to know who the booking was for, how they’d pay, and what happens if insurance says no.
If every designer solved that alone, the rules would drift apart.
So I designed checkout first, and every service built on it.
The developers wanted to finish consults first and generalize later.
I showed them what retrofitting five services would cost, and we agreed to build the shared checkout first.
Options
Each service designs its own checkout · one identical checkout · a shared core that services add to
Decision
The patient, payment switch and payment list stay fixed.
A service can add an option, but not replace the pattern.
Trade-off
Checkout had to be designed before any service flow could finish.
Result
Six services shipped on one checkout pattern.

Pharmacy Delivered medicines

But no service builds its own version.

One status language, wherever it appears
Every status uses the same parts: a tint, an icon, a plain word, and an action when there’s one to take.
Learn it once on an insurance card, and you can read it anywhere in the app.
Covered: green tint, a check, the word Valid.
Not covered: a note that names the next step, tap Self Pay.
A blocker: a red banner with the fix inside it, Update Now.
When there’s no price to show at checkout
The hospital system only creates the fee after the insurer replies, so at checkout there’s no price to show.
Rather than block the booking, checkout says Under Process and notifications do the rest.
Patients still book without knowing the amount.
Honestly, that’s the part I’m least happy with.

Make the price a condition for booking · book now, and let the fee arrive as a state

Patients still commit without knowing the amount.

s: The test took seconds.
Keeping track of it didn’t.
If your cat or dog has diabetes, you test their blood glucose every morning and evening.
The test itself is quick.
What owners struggled with was everything around it: keeping readings in one place, and getting them to the vet before the analyzer overwrote them.
The routine
Owners tested their pet at home every morning and evening, then wrote the reading on paper, in phone notes, or in a spreadsheet.
Before a vet visit, they gathered it all up and photographed it.
The routine’s cost
Writing readings down added work to a routine that was already tiring.
Before a vet visit, owners said they spent 30+ minutes pulling it all together.
The analyzer constraint
The analyzer only keeps seven days of readings.
If owners didn’t sync in time, older readings were overwritten and lost.
The design challenge
Make readings quick to record, make it obvious when data needs syncing, and help owners hand the vet an organized history.
How it worked before
Take a reading While handling the pet
Record it On paper, in notes, or in a spreadsheet
Gather records Before an appointment
Share with the vet As photos or printouts
30+ min to prepare one vet visit (self-reported)
The analyzer keeps only seven days of readings
Day 1 Overwritten
Day 2 Overwritten
Day 3 In memory
Day 4 In memory
Day 5 In memory
Day 6 In memory
Day 7 In memory
Day 8 In memory
Day 9 In memory
Skip syncing for nine days, and the first two days are gone, including readings a vet uses to adjust insulin.
I started in people’s homes, not in Figma
Before I designed anything, I wanted to see what actually happens around a reading, not just the moment someone types a number in.
So I visited owners at home first.
Then I talked to vets, to understand what they do with the records owners bring in.
14-day diary study Six owners, drawn from the 10 interviewees
3 veterinarian interviews How vets review owners’ records
4 competing apps Built for human diabetes; sharing with a vet meant a raw CSV file
Journey map Showed scattered readings and missed syncs
3 usability rounds Five participants in each round
Evidence Insight Design decision
Usability, Round 1
Setup asked for too much before people could do the one thing they came for.
Let people log a first reading right after sign-up, before any other setup.
Decision 1
Owners hold the analyzer in one hand and a restless pet in the other.
Diary study
Logging had to compete with looking after the pet.
Keep entry short, with as little typing as possible.
Decision 2
The analyzer retained seven days of readings before overwriting older data.
Hardware constraint
Owners needed to see at a glance whether their data was up to date.
Show sync status clearly, with a way to fix it.
Decision 3
Veterinarians reviewed trends against a pet’s target range.
Vet interviews
A number on its own doesn’t tell you much.
Show readings against the pet’s target range, with meals and insulin.
Decision 4
All six diary participants set up phone alarms at the start.
By the end of week one, all six were ignoring them.
Diary study
Generic alarms are easy to tune out.
Make each reminder about a specific pet and task.
Decision 5
None of the three vets used a shared app with owners.
They all got records by email or messaging.
Vet interviews
Sharing had to fit how clinics already work.
Start with a PDF report instead of the planned vet portal.
Decision 6
One rule behind every decision
Everything I learned pointed the same way.
Owners didn’t need another task.
They needed the routine they already had to take less effort.
That meant four things: get people to a first reading fast, cut the typing, make sync status obvious, and keep records ready for the vet.
The guiding principle
Fit the app into the care routine owners already have.
What the routine looks like with PetTrackr
Take a reading As part of the existing care routine
Sync or log it From the analyzer, or with date and time prefilled
Review it in context Against the pet’s target range
Share the history As a PDF, through the device’s sharing options
< 1 min to generate and share a report
First, get people to a reading
The original onboarding had seven steps.
People had to set up almost everything, including Bluetooth pairing, before they could log a single reading.
In Round 1, 2 of 5 people didn’t make it through, and 4 of 5 got stuck on pairing.
Round 1 · seven steps
Create account
Pet profile
Species
Target range
Insulin dose
Bluetooth pairing
Notifications
Revised flow

Intro and sign-up 3 short intro screens (each can be skipped), then an account, because readings are saved in the cloud First reading Log a blood glucose reading Later Pet details, pairing, and reminders
Options
Shorten every form · make all setup optional · move one useful action ahead of the rest
Decision
Keep the account step, because readings are saved in the cloud.
Then take people straight to logging their first reading.
Trade-off
Setup is unfinished at first: pet details, pairing and reminders come later.
Sign-up still comes first.
The guest flow in Section 08 looks at removing it.
Result
In testing, completion went from 3 of 5 (60%) in Round 1 to 8 of 9 (89%) across Rounds 2 and 3, above our 85% target.
One Round 3 participant never got to onboarding.
Introduction screens explain the app and can be skipped.
Each of the three introduction screens has a Skip option.
Right after sign-up, the first task is one blood glucose reading.
Making logging a quick confirmation, not a form
In the diary study, owners were logging with the analyzer in one hand and a restless pet in the other.
At that moment, a long form just gets in the way.
Options
A full entry form · a quick-add shortcut · a shorter form with known information already filled in
Decision
Fill in the date and time automatically, so the glucose number is the only thing to enter.
Trade-off
Notes on food, stress, or activity are optional, so some readings get saved without that context.
Result
Under 30 seconds, timed in usability sessions from tapping “Add reading” to saving.
On paper, diary participants reported three to five minutes.
Date and time are prefilled; the reading is the main input.
Round 3 enlarged the reading field.
The selected pet stays visible during logging.
Saved readings appear in that pet’s logbook.
Making sync status impossible to miss
I wanted the app to sync in the background, so owners never had to think about it.
But phones limit background Bluetooth, and the analyzer’s firmware couldn’t support it reliably in the first release.
Universal Biosensors and the developers put automatic sync on hold.
If owners had to sync themselves, they should at least always see when they last did.
Options
Background sync (deferred) · sync when opening the app · visible status with a reconnect option
Decision
The app syncs when it’s open and the analyzer is nearby.
Each analyzer shows when it last synced, with a way to reconnect.
Trade-off
Owners still have to open the app near the analyzer to keep their records up to date.
Result
Owners can now see their sync status instead of guessing.
We didn’t measure whether this reduced lost readings.
Each analyzer shows its last sync time.
Pairing is introduced after the initial logging flow.
The empty state explains how to connect an analyzer.
Showing each reading against the pet’s target range
Owners couldn’t tell whether a number like 140 was good or bad.
The vets I spoke to never read a number on its own.
They judged it against that pet’s target range, so I made the chart do the same.
Options
A table · a line chart · a chart with target-range zones
Decision
Shade the chart by the pet’s own range, and mark meals and insulin on the same timeline.
Daily and weekly views use the same zones.
Trade-off
The zones depend on the vet’s target range.
Until an owner enters it, the chart shows the line without zones and prompts them to add it.
Result
In testing, the median time to answer “Was this morning’s reading in range?” went from 22 seconds (number list, Round 1) to 7 seconds (zone chart, Round 2).
The daily chart places readings against low, in-range, and high zones.
The pet profile stores the target range used by the chart.
The weekly view adds minimum, average, and maximum values.
Reminders that say which pet and what’s due
All six diary participants set phone alarms at the start.
By the end of week one, all six were ignoring them.
A reminder only helps if it says exactly what to do, and for which pet.
Scope
Blood glucose checks, meals, insulin, and exercise, for each pet
Decision
Each notification names the pet and the task, and owners can mark a task as done.
Trade-off
Reminders follow a schedule the owner sets.
Adaptive reminders that learn each pet’s routine were put on hold.
Result
Each pet gets its own schedule.
We didn’t measure the effect on completed tasks separately.
The selected pet’s reminders appear in one schedule, and owners can mark a task as done.
Notifications identify the pet and the task.
Starting with a PDF the vet can actually use
Universal Biosensors had planned a portal for vets.
But none of the three vets I spoke to used a shared app with owners; records came in by email or messaging.
So I suggested starting with a PDF that owners could send the usual way.
Universal Biosensors agreed and moved the portal to phase 2.
Universal Biosensors planned A veterinary portal I recommended, the client agreed A PDF report owners can share The three vets’ clinics used Email or messaging, not shared apps
The trade-off Vets only see what owners choose to send
Without a portal, vets don’t have ongoing access, though owners can send a report any time between visits.
The result Visit prep dropped from 30+ minutes (self-reported) to under 1 minute to create and share a 14-day PDF (timed in testing).
Owners pick a period, and the report is built from the logbook.
No photos, no retyping.
Pick a time frame; the start date fills in from it (changed after Round 3).
Share through email, messaging, or other available device options.
What three rounds of testing changed
I ran three rounds of usability testing, five people each.
Round 1 covered the original onboarding, Round 2 the rebuilt onboarding and the zone chart, and Round 3 logging and reports.
The big changes are in the decisions above.
These are the smaller ones, plus what’s still open.
Design Finding Design response Result
Logging and report screens
People mistapped the reading field one-handed, and had to set report dates manually.
Made the reading field bigger, and the report’s start date now fills in from the time frame.
Changed after Round 3, but not retested.
Client review rounds
Client feedback came back as a numbered list.
Put each updated screen right next to the comment it answered.
Every requested change could be checked in one pass.
What’s still unresolved
Rule-based Adaptive
Adaptive reminders were put on hold Deferred
The shipped version uses the owner’s own schedule.
It doesn’t adapt to how each pet’s routine actually runs.
Roboto Montserrat Gilroy
Too many typefaces Not fixed
The design system ended up with three typefaces: Roboto, Montserrat, and Gilroy.
I didn’t consolidate them before handoff, and it’s the first thing I’d clean up.
Status and reconnect Automatic
Automatic sync is still on hold Deferred
The app only syncs when it’s open near the analyzer.
See Decision 3.
Keeping client feedback easy to check
What you’re looking at
Universal Biosensors sent feedback as a numbered list.
I placed each comment right above the screen it referred to, with the updated design underneath.
1 The numbered comment The client’s comment, numbered, above the screen it affects.
2 The updated screen Because each revision sits with its comment, it’s easy to see what changed and why.
Three of four goals met in testing
At kickoff, we agreed on four goals.
Testing showed we met three.
The fourth, whether people keep using the app, needs real usage data that I don’t have yet.
Below, “timed” means measured in testing and “self-reported” means owners told us.
Met At least 85% onboarding completion
8 of 9 (89%) in Rounds 2 and 3, up from 3 of 5 (60%) in Round 1
Met Log a reading in under 60 seconds
Under 30 seconds (timed), down from 3–5 minutes on paper (self-reported)
Met Generate a vet report without re-entering records
Under 1 minute to generate and share a 14-day PDF (timed), down from 30+ minutes (self-reported)
Not measured Better seven-day tracking continuation than paper
Not measured yet.
We never defined what to compare against, or what would count as success.
What I’d measure next
Continued logging Whether owners record another reading for the same pet seven days after their first entry.
Synchronization Time between successful syncs, and whether readings are lost before transfer.
Report sharing How often reports are created and shared.
Knowing whether vets actually use them would need follow-up research.
Reminder follow-through Completed tasks compared with scheduled tasks.
Four things I’d carry into my next project
Looking back, these are the lessons that changed how I work, not just how this app turned out.
The last one is the one I think about most.
Then, on this project Now
The original flow made owners do a lot of setup before they could log a single reading.
I look for the first useful action early, and question which setup steps really need to come before it.
The diary study showed why short entry mattered: people were handling a pet and a device at the same time.
I pay attention to where and when something gets used, not only to the screen itself.
03 Specific reminders are still a guess until measured
Reminders shipped without any way to see whether care tasks actually got done.
A well-reasoned design still needs proof.
Next time, I’d check whether it improves task completion.
04 Agree on how to measure retention before launch
Retention was a kickoff goal that ended without a number.
I’d agree with engineering on what to track, what to compare against, and what success looks like, before launch.
What’s next: logging before creating an account
Right now, the app still asks for an account first, because readings are saved in the cloud.
The next step goes further: a guest flow where owners pick a country, accept the terms, and start logging right away, then move their records into an account later.
These are concepts, not shipped work.
Guest start concept: select a country and accept the terms before continuing.
Account connection concept: identify existing guest records when creating an account.
Data transfer concept: show progress while guest records transfer to the account.

s: When a press was waiting on a certificate, the customer was waiting on an email
Ordering ink was the easy part.
Everything after it meant emailing an account manager and waiting: certificates, order updates, invoices, stock counts.
Sometimes a printing press sat idle in the meantime.
Who
Printers and packaging converters who order, stock and pay for ink.
What went wrong
Every certificate, order update, invoice and stock count went through an account manager.
Why it mattered
A compliance document took 24 to 48 hours.
On one site visit, production stopped 3 times in 2 hours while the team waited for a certificate.
The UX challenge
Let customers answer their own questions after they’ve placed an order, starting from the order they hold.
The loop
Needs a certificate Or an order update, or an invoice copy
Emails the account manager Then calls to chase it
Account manager searches Internal systems and inboxes
Reply by email A PDF or a status update
Every request took account-manager time away from other work.
I went to the factory floor, not just meeting rooms
The first thing I wanted to understand was what happens after an order is placed.
Interviews told me what customers asked for.
Site visits showed me what happened when they didn’t get it.
Two usability rounds then showed which structure actually worked.
Each round had six customer participants.
Journey map 11 friction points
Evidence Insight Design decision
14 of 14 customers raised documents and order status without being asked.
Interviews
The real work starts after the order is placed.
Five self-serve jobs at the center of the portal: orders, consignment stock, invoices, certificates, and support.
The strategy
Nobody found their last certificate in the library.
Usability, Round 1
Customers think in orders, not document types.
Start from the order.
Decision 01
A typical thread about one consignment ran past 20 emails.
Interviews and journey map
A stock update was one job, split across many messages.
One screen, one submit, a status per product.
Decision 02
4 of 12 participants named support first, without being asked.
Testing feedback
A problem on the press can’t wait for an email.
Chat answers plus tracked tickets.
Decision 03
Large PDFs on slow, shared factory networks.
Engineering flow review
A download that sits at zero looks broken.
Three download states on every file.
Decision 04
Make the order the way in
Everything pointed the same way.
Customers don’t think in document types.
They think about what they already have: an order or a delivery.
So the design starts there.
The five after-order jobs sit one step from the order, and every request shows its status, so nobody has to email to ask.
The principle
Start from what the customer already holds: an order, a shipment, a batch.
The journey we designed for
The portal
Needs a certificate The same questions
Opens the order Orders, stock, invoices, support
Requests or downloads it By site, product and batch
Follows the status Requests and tickets show progress
Self-serve no account manager in the loop
Starting from the order, not a document library
The brief asked for a document library, so that’s what we tested first.
In Round 1, nobody could find the certificate for their last delivery in it.
People knew their order, not the document type.
So I rebuilt the structure around the order.
Options
The document library from the brief · a structure built around the order
Decision
Make the order the way in.
Documents live on the shipment they came with.
Trade-off
It cost three sprints of rework, late in the project.
The library stayed, but only for documents not tied to an order.
Result
Round 1: nobody found the certificate for their last delivery.
Round 2: everyone did.

Safety Data Sheets
Technical Data Sheets

Orders

Certificates of Analysis
Request by site › product › batch
100% found it in Round 2
The status sits beside the product name.
One order, several deliveries, each with its own row.
View PDF, Download and Track live on the shipment.
Stock updates on one screen
Consignment stock is ink that sits at the customer’s site until it’s used.
Keeping Flint’s count up to date meant email threads that often ran past 20 messages.
So I put the whole job on one screen, with a single submit.
Options
The email thread as it was · one screen with one submit
Decision
Both counts side by side, one figure per product, and one submit for everything.
Trade-off
The screen is dense.
A status on every product and a full change history help people keep track.
Result
Not measured on its own.
Flint’s calculated stock beside the customer’s usage, so gaps show early.
Stock levels or usage, then one figure per product.
Every product goes to Flint in one action.
An icon per row, with a legend above.
Submitted or Not Submitted, in words as well as color.
Every change, with who made it and when.
Making the case for support, which wasn’t in the brief
Support wasn’t in the brief.
It was meant to stay with account managers, and Flint’s sales team worried about losing that contact.
But in testing, 4 of 12 participants brought it up first, without being asked.
A problem on the press can’t wait for an email.
So I wrote a business case that kept account managers in the loop on every request.
Options
Leave support with account managers, as briefed · chat answers plus tracked tickets
Decision
A Technical Support Agent for common problems, and a Support Hub for tracked tickets.
Trade-off
It added scope late, and Flint’s team has to keep the answers current.
Result
Signed off in acceptance testing.
Ask the agent.
Common printing problems come first.
Not solved?
Not solved?
Raise a ticket and follow it to resolved.
Making large downloads look alive on slow networks
Before the build, the engineering lead pointed out something I’d missed.
On slow factory networks, a large PDF can sit at zero for a while, and a download that looks stuck looks broken.
So I gave every download the same three clear states.
Options
No visible state, as first designed · three explicit states
Decision
Downloading, Downloaded, and Failed with Try again, on every file.
Trade-off
Three more states to design and build for every download.
Result
After launch, the fix customers praised most.
Start Tap Download
On any certificate, data sheet or invoice
State 1 · Downloading CoA_5055461.pdf
Progress keeps moving, so it never looks stuck.
State 2 · Downloaded Done, with the file name
A clear confirmation, so nobody clicks twice.
State 3 · Failed Says what went wrong, then Try again
Try again goes straight back to Downloading.
Nothing stalls silently.
Try again → back to Downloading
What changed after testing, and what’s still open
Most of what testing changed is in the decisions above.
Some problems only showed up once the portal was in real use.
Here’s what we changed, and what still needs fixing.
Design Finding Design response Result
One delivery to confirm per product
Real sites get several deliveries for one product.
Each delivery is confirmed on its own.
Reworked in a maintenance release.
What remained unresolved
Issue What’s wrong Status
Status tag contrast
Every tag has a word, so color is never the only signal.
But none reach 4.5:1: Not Submitted 2.4:1, Open 2.9:1, Closed 2.7:1, Submitted 3.0:1.
The proposed colors reach 4.9:1 to 5.4:1.
Not fixed

White on #25B67C is 2.6:1, while #17805A reaches 4.9:1.
Icon-only buttons also need accessible names, and download states should be announced to screen readers.
Not fixed
Account approval wait
New accounts can wait 48 hours or more for approval.
I designed a waiting state, but the wait itself wasn’t solved.
Not solved
What was signed off, and what nobody measured
Customers signed off all three success criteria in acceptance testing, so the portal does the jobs it was built for.
What nobody tracked after launch is whether fewer requests reached account managers.
That’s the number I’d most like to have.

Three things I took away
The best idea in this portal came from a test that failed.
Looking back, these are the lessons from that, and from the things I missed.
Lesson Then, on this project Now
The library from the brief failed in Round 1, because customers think in orders, not document types.
I start every structure from what the customer already holds: an order, a shipment, a batch.
We assumed one delivery per product.
Real sites get several, and a maintenance release had to fix it.
On site visits, I walk through a real week of deliveries, not a single order.
Whether fewer requests reached account managers was never tracked.
I agree the after-launch number and its baseline at kickoff.
A future direction: the first two days
New accounts can wait 48 hours or more for approval.
These concepts let customers complete their profile while they wait, and show how far approval has got, with a way to raise a request.
Complete the profile while the account is being approved.
A waiting state that says how far approval has got, with a way to raise a request.
